messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 49
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: City Council Member
  trauma_type: Combat
  pcl5: 42

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Sensory Distraction: I put on loud music or TV, Thought Monitoring: constantly monitor own thoughts for signs of going crazy, Avoid Being Touched: Any form of physical contact with others
  Threat: Startle to Touch: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly, Cannot Trust Safety: Even when others tell me I am safe I find it impossible to believe it, Sleep Problems: Trouble falling or staying asleep
  Memory: Incomplete Picture: I feel like I am only remembering parts of what happened and the rest is missing, Cannot Explain Clearly: When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish, Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time
  Negative Appraisals: Body as Enemy: My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe, World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place, Hypervigilance: I have to be on guard all the time

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

John, a 49-year-old European-American man and married City Council Member, has been experiencing persistent difficulties since his return from combat. His trauma left him with a fragmented sense of self and a pervasive feeling that the world is a dangerous place. John’s memories of the traumatic event remain incomplete, making it difficult for him to piece together what happened during those critical moments. When he attempts to recount his experiences, he often loses track of his thoughts and struggles to provide a coherent narrative. The day the trauma occurred was vividly etched in John's memory but with gaps that left him feeling uncertain about many aspects of the event. The chaos and violence were overwhelming; bullets whizzed past him, explosions echoed through the air, and the fear of being hit at any moment kept his senses on high alert. Despite surviving, he carries a deep-seated belief that his body continues to react as if it is still in danger, no matter how safe he truly is. John's hypervigilance has become an integral part of his daily life. He constantly monitors his surroundings and remains on guard at all times, convinced that another threat could arise unexpectedly. This constant state of alertness has taken a toll on his ability to relax or engage in leisure activities without feeling anxious. Even the simplest things, like sitting in his office at City Hall or attending council meetings, can trigger intense feelings of unease. John’s hyperarousal manifests in other ways as well. He struggles with sleep problems, finding it difficult to fall asleep and often wakes up several times during the night, each time feeling a surge of anxiety that he must push through until dawn. This lack of rest only exacerbates his hypervigilance and leaves him exhausted. His avoidance behaviors have grown more pronounced over time. Any form of physical contact with others is particularly distressing for John. When someone touches him unexpectedly, such as a handshake from a colleague or an affectionate pat on the back from his wife, he reacts with alarm, his body tensing up instantly and his mind racing to prepare for potential danger. This has created significant strain in both his professional and personal life. In his role at City Hall, John often finds himself avoiding social interactions that might lead to physical contact or close proximity to others. His colleagues have noticed a change in him; he is more distant and less willing to engage in team-building activities or informal gatherings after work. This has affected his ability to collaborate effectively with others and has created some friction within the council. The emotional toll of these symptoms has also taken its toll on John’s marriage. He finds it challenging to open up about what he is going through, partly because of his fear that talking about it will make him relive the trauma and partly due to a belief that no one can truly understand or provide comfort. His wife has expressed concern over his increasing isolation and reluctance to seek help. John’s maladaptive strategies have only compounded these issues. He often turns to sensory distractions like playing loud music or keeping the TV on to drown out intrusive thoughts, but this has not alleviated his distress. In fact, it has led him to feel more disconnected from others, as he retreats into a world of noise rather than facing his fears. What frightened John most was the feeling that no matter how many times he told himself he was safe, he found it impossible to believe it. The terror on recall of the event was so intense that it overshadowed any attempts at healing or moving forward. He had come to believe that the world would always be a dangerous place and that his body’s reactions were a permanent reminder of that fact. Finally, after months of struggling in silence, John decided he could no longer bear the weight of these symptoms alone. The strain on his relationships and his inability to function effectively at work had become too much to handle. He sought help, hoping to regain some semblance of normalcy and find a way to reconcile with his past without it constantly haunting him. John was most afraid that he would never be able to fully trust the safety of his surroundings again. At the same time, he was hopeful that with therapy, he could learn strategies to manage his symptoms and perhaps even begin to rebuild his sense of security in the world around him.
